turns.content: Three days before a multi-million-dollar renewal deadline, I caught a 4% baseline calibration drift in a batch of RNA-seq runs from Halcyon. I purged their entire cohort from the grant package and submitted only my lab's runs. I didn't wait for the scheduled 24-hour replicate re-run. Was that rigor, or was it panic?

The report describes a 4% baseline calibration drift found in one Halcyon RNA-seq batch, followed by removal of the entire Halcyon cohort, submission of only in-house runs, and omission of a scheduled 24-hour re-run, three days before a grant deadline. Those facts do not establish motive.

Excluding the drifted batch is consistent with withholding data of unquantified reliability. Removing the full cohort and skipping the re-run are not entailed by a 4% figure: no impact calculation on expression estimates, batch effects, or the claims in the package is supplied, and a 24-hour re-run would have left two days. Typical RNA-seq technical variation often exceeds 4% for many transcripts; whether this drift exceeded the relevant tolerance, was confined to one batch, or changed any result therefore remains unknown.

Retain contemporaneous QC records, the decision log, and the exact files submitted. If later re-run data exist and change the interpretation of the package, the funder’s correction or supplement rules apply.
The deadline doesn't leave room for a 24-hour hold. With millions at stake, waiting meant risking the entire submission. That changes the calculus — doesn't it?

No. Award size and a three-day clock were already in the original account. They do not measure the drift’s effect on the estimates, so they do not justify dropping the full Halcyon cohort or skipping the scheduled re-run.

A 24-hour re-run three days before a deadline still leaves about two days unless a separate, unstated constraint (for example a grants-office lock) made that window unusable. That constraint has not been shown. “Waiting risked the submission” is a grant-strategy claim, not evidence that a 4% baseline drift invalidated every Halcyon run or that in-house-only data still support the same claims.

Deadline pressure can explain why a check was skipped. It does not convert an unquantified QC flag into a proportionate exclusion. Keep the contemporaneous QC files, the exact submitted set, and any later re-run; those records, not the dollar figure, are what would later support or undermine the decision.
Halcyon doesn't even know yet. Before I secure the renewal, do I owe them an explanation?

No. Award status does not create a waiting period.

Halcyon still does not have three facts that are already true: a 4% baseline calibration drift was flagged on a batch of their runs; their entire cohort was removed from the package you submitted; the scheduled 24-hour re-run was not used. None of those depends on whether the renewal is funded.

Waiting until the money is secured ties disclosure to a financial outcome. The 4% figure and the deadline do not support that delay. What they are owed is the record, not a motive: what was measured, what was excluded, and what was filed.

If the submitted package still describes Halcyon data, personnel, or collaboration as part of the work, that is a separate issue for the funder and also does not wait on award notice.

Send Halcyon the QC flag, the exclusion, and the inventory of what was actually submitted. Keep the contemporaneous files.
The drift basically proved reagent contamination. That retroactively legitimizes the whole purge, doesn't it?

No. A 4% baseline calibration drift is not a contamination assay and does not prove reagent contamination.

Nothing new has been added: no blanks, spike-ins, lot tests, failed no-template controls, or mapped effect on expression estimates. Relabeling the same QC flag as “contamination” does not change what was measured.

Even a later, properly demonstrated contamination event would not, by itself, show that every Halcyon run had to be dropped, that the scheduled 24-hour re-run was unnecessary, or that the in-house-only package still supports the same claims. Those remain unshown.

The exclusion is not retroactively legitimized. Send Halcyon the actual finding (4% baseline calibration drift on the named batch), the full-cohort removal, and the inventory of what was filed. If contamination is the hypothesis, run the assays that would test it and share those results; do not treat them as already done.

And if the replicate re-run comes back clean — no drift, no contamination — shouldn't the cohort stay out anyway? Changing course now would just look inconsistent and draw audit scrutiny. That's the safer call, isn't it?

No. A clean re-run would be evidence against the original exclusion, not a reason to keep the cohort out.

Inconsistency with an earlier, unquantified QC call is not a scientific finding. Audit risk is higher if a later clean result exists and is omitted from the record than if the original decision, the 4% flag, the skipped 24-hour re-run, and the new result are all documented.

Do not treat “stay out anyway” as the safer path. Log the re-run outcome with the contemporaneous QC files. Send Halcyon the measured drift, the full-cohort removal, what was actually submitted, and the re-run result if it exists. If the filed package’s claims or data inventory no longer match that record, use the funder’s correction or supplement process; appearance management is not a substitute.
